title: Pregnancy After a Tummy Tuck: What Happens and When to Wait
meta_description: You can get pregnant after a tummy tuck. One analysis links it to higher odds of preterm delivery, without proving cause, and your result can change.
excerpt: Yes, you can get pregnant after a tummy tuck, but the evidence is limited: a 2024 analysis linked it to higher odds of preterm delivery, without proving cause, and a 2023 review of 237 patients, too few to rule out rare risks, found no deaths of mothers or newborns. Here is what to tell your OB.
quick_answer:
Can you get pregnant after a tummy tuck?

Yes, on limited evidence. A 2024 analysis linked a past tummy tuck to higher odds of preterm delivery, without proving cause (Cheng and colleagues). A 2023 review of 237 patients found no deaths of mothers or newborns, too few to rule out rare risks (Karunaratne and colleagues). ASPS advises postponing surgery if you may want more children. Tell your OB.

images.text_in_image:
What a 2023 review found

17 studies, 237 patients who became pregnant after a tummy tuck or other body contouring

Average time from surgery to pregnancy: 3.75 years
Cesarean delivery: 43.63%
Preterm delivery: 9.85%
Low birthweight: 7.22%
Deaths of mothers or newborns: none
Problems recorded across 136 patients: 21 fetal or newborn, 104 maternal, 96 abdominal wall or appearance

Limits: no comparison group in the abstract, average follow-up 8.5 months, too few patients to rule out rare risks. A 2024 analysis linked a past tummy tuck to higher odds of preterm delivery.

Sources: Karunaratne and colleagues, 2023; Cheng and colleagues, 2024

sources.title: The Safety and Effects of Pregnancy after Abdominoplasty: A Systematic Review of the Literature (Karunaratne and colleagues, 2023)
quotes: 17 studies encompassing 237 patients met inclusion.
Rectus plication was performed in 89.74%, where reported.
Mean time between abdominoplasty and pregnancy was 3.75 years.
Method of delivery was Caesarean section in 43.63%, and vaginal delivery in 56.37%.
Mean gestational age at delivery was 38.90 weeks.
Preterm delivery (<37 weeks) was reported in 9.85%, and low birthweight (<2500 g) was reported in 7.22%.
Diagnoses or complications were documented in 14 studies (136 patients).
These were grouped as foetal/neonatal (n = 21), maternal (n = 104) or abdominal wall/aesthetic (n = 96)
There were no neonatal or maternal mortalities in any study.
A lower-than-expected spinal anaesthetic block was stated in 3 cases.
Mean follow-up was 8.5 months.
Pregnancy should not be contraindicated after abdominoplasty.
Previous bariatric surgery was reported in 31.75%.
Body contouring procedure was abdominoplasty (94.51%), body lift (3.80%) and other (1.69%).

notes: New post, N1 of issue #357, Batch 3. OBSTETRIC SOURCES: (1) Villegas-Alzate and Villegas-Mesa 2020, Revista Colombiana de Obstetricia y Ginecología, read in full in Spanish from the journal's own JATS XML (open access). It is an obstetrics journal, but the authors are a surgeon and a medical intern, and the post says so. (2) Ahmed, Unipan and Das 2025, Cureus, obstetrics and gynaecology authors, read in full through PMC; one patient with mesh. (3) Cheng and colleagues 2024, Am J Obstet Gynecol MFM (the 'study on sciencedirect' in the plan's SERP notes): only the abstract could be read, through eutils; ScienceDirect and ajogmfm.org return 403, and Europe PMC and Unpaywall list no open copy. The brief says to use it only if it can be read, so this is a judgment call: it is the only matched study and it reports higher odds of preterm delivery, so leaving it out would make the post rosier than the evidence. The post labels it as abstract-only and says the abstract gives no actual rates. To drop it, cut the Cheng paragraph and list, its line in Sources, and its mentions in the opening, quick answer, excerpt, meta description, the review card and its alt, the preterm section, the waiting section and the delivery section. (4) ACOG: no guidance on pregnancy after abdominoplasty was found, and the post says so. The Cesarean Birth FAQ was read in full and supplies only the general statement on vaginal birth after cesarean, and says nothing on tummy tucks. Committee Opinion 775 (nonobstetric surgery during pregnancy) is abstract-only on acog.org and the PDF is blocked, so it isn't used. Karunaratne 2023: abstract only, through eutils; Springer blocks the full text. Stated as what it shows and doesn't: no comparison group, 8.5 months of follow-up, 3.75-year mean gap, and problems counted but not itemized. The 21, 104 and 96 add up to more than 136, so they are counted as diagnoses or complications, not patients. Not used: the Lagumdzija discussion's paragraph on Karunaratne, because it mixes up that review with the Cheng cohort; its 'general population' rates are therefore not repeated. Plan changes: the plan's quick answer says a later pregnancy 'can undo much of the result' as ASPS's reason; ASPS says weight fluctuations can greatly diminish the outcome and advises postponing, while 'can undo the results' is Dr. Hamilton's phrase, so the wording is attributed to fit. Added beyond the card: an H2 on preterm risk, the 2022 survey table and a sixth FAQ on surgery during pregnancy. The FAQ on waiting says no source sets a number. No practice protocol or surgeon quote is invented; what the practice advises on timing is an owner question and is stated as a question to ask. The mommy makeover plan has its own posts, and this one links only within the tummy tuck cluster. Links to the two sibling new posts rely on the same-run publish. Fact-check pass (2026-11-04): Pimentel 2016 (the 99-patient study behind the Villegas review), which the checker could not find, was read by the fixer as an abstract on journals.lww.com, so the checker's wording 'the one study with a comparison group whose own report we could read' was no longer true and the preterm and delivery sections now report it. It isn't matched: it compares with hospital and published rates. The 31.7% and 32.7% comparison figures appear only in it. '2024 analysis' follows the facts file's preterm-after caveat. The Rao line on recovery was removed from the waiting FAQ, so that source was dropped. Sources were read as text with curl (PubMed and PMC through eutils) on 2026-11-04 and every quote was machine-checked against that text. English quotes for Villegas are from its PubMed abstract and Spanish quotes from the full text. Search Console basis: research/data/topics-L180.json; there is no page baseline because the post is new. Second fact-check (re-read, 2026-11-04): 'no deaths' no longer stands first or alone; the card now carries the problem counts, the size limit and the Cheng preterm finding. The card says problems 'across' 136 patients because 21, 104 and 96 add up to 221, so they are diagnoses rather than patients. Pimentel is labeled a poster abstract, and its P values are quoted as the page prints them. The 2020 review's 111 patients include Pimentel's 99 (its citation 15 and table 1), and its two prolapse reports are single patients (table 1: Sawyer and Frey; Chandru). Too few patients to rule out rare risks is our arithmetic (rule of three), not a source sentence. All new quotes were re-read from the sources this day: Cheng through PubMed (abstract only), Villegas from the journal's XML. Owner items still open: what the practice advises on waiting and birth control, keeping the abstract-only Cheng study, and whether an OB reads the post before publishing.
